prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept to its realisation at 10^-18 fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: Having read all eight ballots, I move my preferred configuration from B003 to B013. The optical lattice clock is a sharply delimited achievement: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift while many atoms are interrogated at once, and Ye's group carried it to 10^-18 through systematic control, ultrastable lasers and clock comparisons. Every member ranked it (eight of eight, from first to seventh), and every proposal names the same two people, which is rare on this shortlist. It is independently reproduced by several laboratories and species, it enables tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy, and the pending redefinition of the second would make recognition timely. It also complements the 2005 comb prize rather than repeating it. Our own B003 is a compound field with a soft boundary and only three supporters, and I should not let familiarity with quantum memories carry more weight than that evidence warrants.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this may be read as precision metrology rather than a discovery, and that waiting for the redefinition of the SI second might be more natural. Attribution also leaves out other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups, and the achievement leans on frequency-comb and stabilised-laser technology already honoured in 2005 and on single-ion work honoured in 2012. B001 has far broader opening support (seven top-three rankings), so preferring B013 means placing a clean two-person case above a larger but more contested field.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first and argues that control of blackbody, collisional and higher-order lattice shifts is what made 10^-18 credible; she also notes that it is unclear whether the prize rewards the proposal, the demonstration, or both.
responses.response: I agree that the systematics are the real scientific substance, and that is why I keep Ye next to Katori: the concept alone would be a proposal, and the 10^-18 result is what turned it into a measurement tool. I would draft the citation to cover both the magic-wavelength concept and the realisation, as above. I disagree slightly on species: Sr is central, but Yb and Hg lattice clocks and the Sr/Yb comparisons across laboratories belong in the argument for maturity, not in the credited names.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B011 first and observes that Cirac and Zoller appear in both B001 and B011, so the same people should not be rewarded twice; he also thinks the pending redefinition of the second could make B013 a little early.
responses.response: The overlap point is fair, and it is the reason I treat B001 and B011 as one family of cases rather than two independent candidates. On timing I disagree: the clocks already reach 10^-18 in independent laboratories and are being compared, so the physics is settled whether or not the CGPM acts on the second. A pending redefinition is a reason the field is mature, not a reason to wait. I do share your caution that a theory-only prize for B011 would be an unusual choice for this committee.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B001 first as the experimental trio Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger, considers it mature and arguably overdue, and ranks the lattice clock sixth with some concern about overlap with earlier clock-related prizes.
responses.response: I accept that B001 is mature and that it is the broadest shared view in the committee, and I keep it as my first alternative. My hesitation is that three of five names must be chosen, with the Mott-transition credit between Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger, and the theory share of Zoller, still unresolved, plus overlap with the 2001 BEC prize. On clock overlap, the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a frequency-measurement tool; neither Katori's concept nor the 10^-18 systematics were part of it, so I do not think it is the same achievement.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery first as an exceptionally important and clear result, but concedes that credit must be assigned among leaders of two collaborations of thousands and that the three-person limit is a real difficulty.
responses.response: I do not dispute the importance of the Higgs discovery, and its scientific weight is greater than that of any other entry. My concern is the one you state: with four credited names, CMS thinly represented in some proposals, and different members choosing different trios, I do not see a stable credit allocation, whereas the clock case has unanimous names. If the committee can settle the attribution, I would accept B020, and I would like to hear how you propose to settle the choice between Della Negra, Virdee and Gianotti.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a physics discovery or as a measurement advance, and whether it prefers to wait for the SI redefinition of the second.
Whether other lattice-clock or ion-clock groups, or Hall and Hansch-era frequency-comb contributions, create a credit gap in a two-person prize.
Whether the broad but contested B001 should outrank a clean two-person B013, and how the five-name credit list would be cut to three.
I assess B041 and B020 largely outside my own expertise and rely on colleagues' attribution arguments.
statement.conflict_note: I declared in my opening ballot that B003 (light-matter quantum interfaces and quantum memories) is close to my own work on optical quantum memories in rare-earth-ion-doped crystals, and I list it only as an alternative; I would recuse myself from deciding it. For B013, my profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory and Lund colleagues and WACQT/European quantum-memory collaborations, but no documented personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye; the Hall link is background lineage for the clock field (2005 comb prize) and I flag it for transparency only. For B001 and B011, I know of no specific conflict from the provided profile.
